Day 5 of answering the questions you’re too scared to ask your accountant 👀💰

What happens if you overcontribute to your TFSA?

First… don’t panic. It happens more often than you think!

If you contribute more than your available TFSA room, the CRA considers the excess amount an overcontribution and you may be charged a 1% tax per month on the excess amount until it’s withdrawn or corrected.

Common ways this happens:
✨ Forgetting you already contributed earlier in the year
✨ Withdrawing from your TFSA and re-contributing too soon (without enough room)
✨ Having multiple TFSA accounts and losing track of contributions

The best first step? Check your actual TFSA contribution room through your CRA My Account before making contributions.

And remember: a TFSA isn’t “tax-free money” if you break the rules but with a little planning, it’s one of the best wealth-building tools available to Canadians 🇨🇦

caption:
Most business owners don’t actually know their cost of capital…
but it’s quietly running the entire show. 👀

Your cost of capital is the price you pay to fund your business.

That could be:
• Interest on debt
• Investor returns
• The return you expect on your own money
• Or even the opportunity cost of not investing elsewhere

It’s basically the “hurdle rate” your business needs to beat.

If your marketing campaign returns 12%…
but your cost of capital is 18%?

You’re technically losing value.

If your expansion earns 25%
and your cost of capital is 10%?

You’re building wealth.

This is why revenue alone doesn’t impress me.
I care about return relative to capital deployed.

Because growth that costs more than it earns
is just expensive stress.

Save this for the next time you’re making a big decision:
👉 “Does this beat my cost of capital?”

That’s how CFOs think.

caption:
5 things all profitable businesses do 👀⬇️:

1. They look at their numbers even when they don’t want to. 
Not daily. Not obsessively. But often enough that nothing gets ignored for months.

2. They deal with small problems early. 
Misclassified expenses. Forgotten subscriptions. Pricing that no longer makes sense. 
They fix it when it’s annoying not when it’s urgent.

3. They plan around cash, not vibes. 
Sales can be up and cash can still feel tight. 
They pay attention to timing, not just totals.

4. They ask questions before something feels wrong. 
They don’t wait until tax season. 
They don’t wait until something breaks.

5. They do a quick money check-in every week. 
Not a deep dive. 
Just enough to know what’s coming in and what’s going out so nothing surprises them.

Profit isn’t luck. It’s habits.

caption:
If you run a business in Canada, GST isn’t optional knowledge.

But most business owners are confused about:

• When to register
• When to charge it
• What they owe CRA
• What they can claim back

So here’s everything you actually need to know about GST.

Save this for later📲

1️⃣ When do you have to register for GST?

You must register once your business earns more than $30,000 in revenue within a 12-month period.

Once you pass this threshold you must:

• Register for a GST/HST number
• Start charging GST on taxable sales
• File GST returns

If you stay under $30K you are considered a small supplier and registration is optional.

2️⃣ What GST rate do you charge?

It depends on the province your customer is in.

Examples:

• Alberta – 5% GST
• Ontario – 13% HST
• BC – 5% GST (plus PST handled separately)

For most online businesses, the rate is based on where the customer lives.

3️⃣ What is an Input Tax Credit (ITC)?

This is the part people miss.

You can claim back the GST you paid on business expenses.

Example:

You collect $1,000 GST from customers
You paid $300 GST on business expenses

You only send $700 to CRA

4️⃣ How often do you file GST?

Most small businesses file annually.

But depending on revenue you may file:

• Annually
• Quarterly
• Monthly

Your filing frequency is assigned by CRA.

5️⃣ What happens if you forget to file?

CRA can charge:

• Late filing penalties
• Interest
• Estimated assessments

Even if you owe nothing, you still need to file.

6️⃣ Pro tip from a CPA

Always move the GST you collect into a separate bank account.

That money is not your revenue.
It belongs to CRA.

Separating it avoids tax-time surprises.

If you’re a business owner trying to understand taxes, follow @hermoneyfinancial for simple financial education.

And save this post for your next GST filing.
